definition: Laborious means requiring long, slow, careful toil.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word laborious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know laborious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Untangling and re-knotting the trawler's half-mile net after every voyage was laborious work that cost the crew a full day in port.
Time-consuming only says a task eats hours; laborious adds toil - the hours are full of slow, careful effort.
Backbreaking outdoes laborious on the body: laborious work wears you down over patient hours, while backbreaking work grinds muscle and spine directly.

Toilsome is the older, plainer word for work full of hard, wearying toil, and it keeps its eye on the effort alone. Laborious adds slowness and care: hours of small, exact steps that wear you down patiently. A toilsome march simply tires you; a laborious audit tires you one line at a time.

Plodding describes the mover, and it faults them as dull — slow, heavy-footed, without spark. Laborious respects the work instead: the task is slow because it demands long, patient, careful toil, not because the worker lacks energy. A plodding lecture drags; a laborious restoration earns its hours.

Laborious means requiring long, slow, careful toil.

Before spreadsheets, the co-op's bookkeeper closed each month the laborious way: seven ledgers reconciled line by line, three evenings of patient checking, and a single slipped digit could send her back to the top of the column.
Laborious emphasizes the slow, grinding quality of work - toil measured in patient hours rather than bursts of strength.
A laborious task is not necessarily heavy; it is long, careful, and wearying.
Laborious points at the toil inside a task: long, slow, effortful.
Its unit-mates divide the territory - arduous stresses that the whole undertaking is difficult and tiring, while strenuous says the demand falls on the body's strength and stamina.
A tax form can be laborious without being strenuous; a sprint is strenuous without being laborious.

The first great dictionary of the county dialect was assembled not in a university but in a farmhouse kitchen.
Its editor, Agnes Hale, spent thirty years sorting paper slips into shoeboxes, each slip carrying one word, one source, one date, copied out in her small exact hand.
Visitors expecting misery found something stranger: Hale called the laborious sorting the best hours of her day, even though it visibly wore her down.
A single entry could demand forty slips compared, re-read, and re-filed before one line of print was settled.
When the volume finally appeared, reviewers marveled that patience on that scale had not simply given out.
